questions.prompt: How does the opposing two-pointer technique reverse an array in place?

options.text: By swapping elements at left and right indices while moving pointers inward.
options.explanation: Right. Pointers start at opposite ends and swap inward until they meet in O(1) space.

options.text: By sorting the array in descending order and copying back to the original.
options.explanation: Sorting rearranges values by size rather than reversing element positions, and takes O(n log n) time.

options.text: By creating a temporary second array and copying items in reverse order.
options.explanation: Creating a second array uses O(n) space and is not an in-place reversal.

options.text: By removing elements from index 0 and appending them back in a loop.
options.explanation: Repeated remove(at: 0) shifts remaining items each step and takes O(n^2) time.

questions.prompt: Why can you not index a Swift string using an integer like text[0]?

options.text: Swift strings are stored as linked lists of single characters in memory.

options.text: Characters are extended grapheme clusters with variable Unicode byte lengths.
options.explanation: Right. Swift must inspect Unicode scalar boundaries rather than assuming fixed offsets.

options.text: Swift strings are immutable structs so no subscript operator is allowed.
options.explanation: Strings allow subscripts using String.Index even when declared with let.

options.text: Subscripts in Swift can only accept String or Enum arguments.

options.text: By sorting all k elements in ascending order at each step.

options.text: By adding the incoming element and subtracting the element leaving the window.

questions.prompt: Why can building a string with result = result + text or mutating shared copies in a loop hurt performance?

options.text: Copying shared or newly created string buffers on each step degrades total time to O(n^2).
options.explanation: Right. Using + or breaking copy-on-write sharing copies the growing string every step instead of growing in place.

options.text: Every + operation converts the entire string to UTF-32 and back again.
options.explanation: Swift stores native strings as UTF-8 and does not convert encodings on +.

options.text: Swift strings allocate a fixed 64-byte buffer that overflows above length 64.
options.explanation: Swift strings grow dynamically and have no 64-character limit.

options.text: The + operator runs a full Unicode normalization pass across every character.
options.explanation: Joining strings checks scalar boundaries at the seam without re-normalizing the whole string.

options.explanation: Creating new strings with + in a loop triggers repeated buffer copies.

options.text: The slice causes a compile error if stored in a struct.
options.explanation: Slices can be stored as stored properties in structs.

options.text: It keeps the entire large parent buffer alive in memory.
options.explanation: Right. Slices share storage with the original buffer, preventing ARC deallocation.

options.text: The slice loses its original indices once the parent leaves scope.

questions.prompt: How does the two-pointer technique reverse an array in place? Explain the pointers and the time and space complexity. Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains one pointer starts at index 0 and another starts at count - 1
Explains pointers swap elements using swapAt and move inward until they meet
States time complexity is O(n) and auxiliary space complexity is O(1)

questions.modelAnswer: The two-pointer technique places one pointer at the start of the array and another at the end. The algorithm swaps the elements at these indices using swapAt and moves both pointers inward until they meet in the middle. This reverses the array in O(n) time and O(1) space because no extra array is allocated.

questions.prompt: Why can you not index a Swift string using an integer subscript like str[0]? How do you work around this in an interview? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains Swift characters are extended grapheme clusters that vary in byte size
Explains Swift requires String.Index to resolve character boundaries safely
Explains converting to Array(string) creates a [Character] array with integer indexing

questions.modelAnswer: Swift strings do not support integer subscripts because characters are extended grapheme clusters that vary in byte length. Swift requires String.Index to traverse Unicode boundaries safely. In coding interviews, you can convert the string to Array(string) to get an array of characters with integer indexing and fast swaps.

questions.prompt: What is an ArraySlice in Swift, and why does accessing slice[0] often cause a crash? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains ArraySlice is a view that shares storage with the original array
Explains ArraySlice retains original indices rather than reindexing from zero
Notes accessing slice[0] when startIndex is greater than 0 triggers an out-of-bounds fatal error

questions.modelAnswer: An ArraySlice is a fast view that shares storage with an original array without copying memory. The slice preserves the exact indices of the original array rather than reindexing from zero. If a slice starts at index 2, calling slice[0] accesses an invalid index and causes a runtime crash.

questions.prompt: How does the sliding window technique find the maximum sum of k consecutive elements in O(n) time? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains computing initial sum of the first k elements
Explains sliding the window by adding the incoming element and subtracting the outgoing element
Notes each step runs in O(1) time, avoiding recalculation and maintaining total O(n) time

questions.modelAnswer: The sliding window technique first computes the sum of the first k elements. As the window slides to the right, it adds the incoming element and subtracts the outgoing element in O(1) time. This rolling update evaluates all subarrays in O(n) total time without recalculating the sum from scratch.

questions.prompt: What is the memory risk of holding a Substring or ArraySlice for a long time, and how do you resolve it? Answer in 2–5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains Substrings and ArraySlices share storage buffers with parent collections
Explains holding a small slice prevents ARC from deallocating the large parent buffer
Explains converting the slice into a new String or Array instance releases the parent buffer

questions.modelAnswer: Substrings and ArraySlices share memory buffers with their original parent collections to avoid copying. Holding a small slice prevents ARC from freeing the entire large parent buffer, which wastes memory. Converting the slice into a dedicated String or Array creates an independent copy and frees the parent memory.
